text: A car has capacity empty seats. It only drives east. You get trips, where each trip is a number of passengers, a from, and a to: pick up that many people at from, and drop them at to. Return true if you can finish every trip.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the car never turns back. So the only question is: at any point on the road, are there ever more than capacity people in the car? And if one group gets off at five and another gets on at five, do they ever share the car?
No. People leave at to, so their seats are free for anyone boarding at that same point.
Got it. A trip covers from up to, but not including, to — half-open. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to a thousand trips. Each trip has one to a hundred passengers. From is less than to, and both are between zero and a thousand. Capacity is up to ten to the fifth.

OK. At most a thousand times a hundred, which is a hundred thousand people at once, so an int is fine. And positions are small: at most a thousand. Let me run through the example: two people from one to five, and three from three to seven. From three to five, both groups ride, so that's five people. With capacity four, false. With capacity five, true. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to check every point on the road and sum the trips that cover it. That's n times a thousand. It works here, but its cost grows with the road length, not with the trips. This problem reminds me of a sweep line over intervals with a min-heap of end points. Sort the trips by pick-up point. Keep a min-heap of drop-off points. Before each pick-up, pop everyone whose drop-off is at or before it. The top of the heap is always the next person to leave. That's n log n.

Here's the plan. One: sort the trips by pick-up point. Two: at each pick-up, drop everyone whose drop-off is at or before it, then board the new group. Three: if the count goes over capacity, return false; otherwise push the drop-off and the count onto the heap. Here, I'm using the min-heap to keep track of who leaves first. I only care about the earliest drop-off, so a heap is enough. One thing worth flagging — the pop check must be less than or equal. People getting off at a point free their seats for people getting on at that same point. With a strict less-than, they'd still be counted, and the car looks full when it isn't. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I sort by the pick-up point, so I see events in road order. The heap stores the drop-off point and the count, with greater, so the smallest drop-off is on top. One thing worth flagging — it's a while, not an if. Several groups can leave before one pick-up. And I check capacity right after boarding. The count only goes up at a pick-up, so that's the only place it can break the limit.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Four trips — two from one to five, three from three to seven, one from five to eight, two from seven to nine — with capacity five; expected true. The two highlighted rows are the key ones: both drops happen exactly at the pick-up point. At five, the group of two leaves first, so one person boards into a car of three. With a strict less-than, nobody drops at five, the count hits six, and it returns false — wrong. Corner cases: back-to-back trips, zero to one then one to two with capacity one, are true. An if instead of a while fails when two groups leave at the same point. Skipping the sort fails when trips come out of order. And checking greater-or-equal rejects a car that's exactly full.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is n log n. The sort is n log n. Each trip is pushed once and popped at most once, so the heap work is n log n in total, even with the inner while. The space complexity is linear, for the heap. Oh, one more thing — since positions are at most a thousand, there's a difference array. Add num at from, subtract it at to, then take a prefix sum and check it never goes over capacity. That's n plus a thousand and one time, a thousand and one cells of space, and no sort. It also gets less-or-equal right for free: at the same point, the minus and the plus land in the same cell. The heap version is the one that still works if positions were too large for an array.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You asked about same-point drop-off and pick-up up front and turned it into less-or-equal. You used a min-heap of drop-offs and explained why the while is still n log n overall. And you used the small position range to offer the linear-time difference array. Good work.
